content:
Moving keyboard shortcuts to a programmable macro keyboard is the most efficient upgrade I’ve ever made.

鍵盤快捷鍵探索之旅

My first exposure to keyboard shortcuts came through macOS’s simple text replacement feature—using @@ for my primary email address, then using similar shortcuts to type full name, address, phone number, zip code, and more.

I then decided to level up, using Keyboard Maestro to set shortcuts to directly open my most-used folders and applications.

From Desktop to Downloads to work-related folders, hitting Fn+F1 through Fn+F6 has become pure muscle memory, eliminating the multiple mouse clicks they previously required. The other function keys are used to launch frequently used applications and websites, plus Keyboard Maestro’s clipboard history switcher.

I then started automating workflows even further, including opening QuickTime and starting a new recording, as well as automatically launching ShurePlus MOTIV when plugging in a specific USB-C microphone.

It wasn’t long before I customized shortcuts for Adobe Audition’s tools, settings, and panel configurations—some of which I quickly moved to the Logitech MX Master mouse for even faster editing.

更進一步

This configuration lasted a long time, until one day, my 9to5Mac colleague Gui Rambo introduced me to a small macro keyboard he’d purchased, with 12 keys and 3 dials. I became immediately intrigued and purchased the same model.

Right out of the box, I discovered it required additional setup to function properly with macOS. Luckily, a GitHub project handled all the complex parts for me, and ChatGPT took care of the rest.

One major benefit of this setup is having a dedicated keyboard for triggering Keyboard Maestro shortcuts, meaning I don’t have to memorize them or worry about ergonomics.

What’s more, since this keyboard offers up to 12 keys per layer across 3 layers, and the dials can also be pressed to function as buttons, I can adopt one mode of operation when working with Adobe Audition, and a completely different mode when working at the operating system level.

When using Adobe Audition, this macro keyboard pairs with the MX Master mouse to let me quickly switch tools, export files (or just the selected portion), apply various effects like volume normalization, compression, de-reverb, de-essing, ripple delete, and more—orders of magnitude faster than using standard keyboard shortcuts, let alone not using shortcuts at all, and the workflow is also much smoother.

At the operating system level, I can switch the same keyboard to another layer to just as easily switch audio inputs, adjust volume, fine-tune screen brightness, mute and unmute the microphone, and open frequently used folders.

Honestly, it took me some time to memorize all these commands, but they became habit faster than I expected. More importantly, when I have to work in an environment without this setup, frankly, my Mac feels broken to me.

Beyond that, macro keyboards come in all shapes and sizes—literally. Shapes, sizes, keys, knobs, lighting colors—you name it. There really is a sense of endless exploration in this space. If your work involves any repetitive actions (and whose doesn’t?), I wholeheartedly recommend giving one a try.
